title: The march to Tabuk
hook: a long march in the heat, and three who stayed behind and told the truth (9:117–118)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the valley of Hunayn: the biggest army yet nearly broke, and a calm was sent down to the ones who stood. Your line was numbers didn't help. Which number did you catch yourself leaning on? Day two hundred eighty-two.

Everyone has missed something they should have gone to, and then had to explain. The easy excuse is right there. The car. The kid was sick. My phone died. In the summer of the ninth year after the hijra, the Prophet ﷺ called for a long march north to Tabuk, near the Byzantine frontier. It was the worst possible time: blazing heat, a long distance, and the dates in Medina just ripening for harvest. Most people went. Some stayed home and later came with excuses. And one man, Ka'b ibn Malik, a veteran who had no excuse at all, kept telling himself he'd catch up tomorrow, and tomorrow, until the army was too far away. Today, what he said when they came home.
screen: `A MARCH IN THE WORST HEAT.` → `SOME CAME BACK WITH EXCUSES.` → `KA'B KEPT SAYING TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Ka'b told the story himself, years later, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it in his own voice. It's one of the longest and most honest first-person accounts in the hadith. When the army returned, the people who had stayed behind lined up with their excuses, more than eighty of them, the report says, and the Prophet accepted what they said on the surface and left their hearts to God. Then it was Ka'b's turn. He said later that he was a good talker, and he could have walked out of there with a story. Instead he said the truth: I had no excuse. I was never stronger or better off than when I stayed behind. The Prophet said: this one has told the truth. Two others, Murarah and Hilal, said the same. And then came the hard part. For fifty days, the community was told not to speak to the three. Ka'b would greet the Prophet and watch to see if his lips moved in reply. His cousin wouldn't answer him. The ninth surah describes it: the earth, vast as it was, became narrow for them, and their own souls felt narrow, until they understood there was no refuge from God except in Him. Then the verses came down: God had turned to them in forgiveness. Ka'b said afterward that the greatest blessing of his life, after Islam itself, was that he didn't lie that day. And the surah adds a line, in Pickthall's words: "be with the truthful."
screen: `KA'B TELLS IT HIMSELF.` · `I HAD NO EXCUSE.` · `FIFTY DAYS OF SILENCE.` · `GOD TURNED TO THEM.` · then, large: `BE WITH THE TRUTHFUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: confess one thing honestly. Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of a small excuse you've been using. The reason you gave for missing something, the version of events you tell that's a little kinder to you than it should be. Just name the true version to yourself, plainly, the way Ka'b did: I had no excuse. If you pray, you can say it to God. If there's a person you owe the truth to, notice who it is, and decide whether you'll tell them after the bell. The bell holds the time.
The march to Tabuk. The long march in the heat, and the three who stayed behind and told the truth. Today's word.
Your line: the truth saved them. Today, when a smooth excuse rises in your mouth, try the plain version instead, and see what happens. Day two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims read Ka'b ibn Malik's account in the hadith collections as a model of repentance through honesty, and 9:119, be with the truthful, is often quoted in sermons on truthfulness.

original.note: Arabic: the truthful ones, from sidq, truthfulness: be with the truthful (9:119).

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a missed battle.
what it means: a man who could have talked his way out chose the truth, and it saved him.
what a scholar hears: Ka'b's first-person hadith in al-Bukhari sits beside 9:117–119, where the three who were left behind are named in the verses of forgiveness.

sources.ref: Qur'an 9:117–118 (the hour of hardship; the three who were left behind, the earth narrow for them, God turns to them)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4418; Sahih Muslim 2769 (Ka'b ibn Malik's account of staying behind from Tabuk)

notes: Pickthall 9:119 excerpt 'be with the truthful' quoted from memory; check.
Details from Ka'b's hadith (more than eighty excuse-makers, fifty days, his cousin Abu Qatadah not answering, watching the Prophet's lips) are from Bukhari 4418 as remembered; confirm.
Ka'b's remark about the greatest blessing after Islam is paraphrased from the end of the hadith; confirm.
Tabuk dated to 9 AH (630 CE); confirm the 'ninth year after the hijra' phrasing.
